# Load Balancing: Interview Answers + Visual Memory Aids

> How to use this file
> 1. Read the **Master Picture** once (the whole concept as one image).
> 2. For each topic: look at the **picture**, say the **interview answer** out loud, then check the **recall hook**.
> 3. Before an interview, redraw the Master Picture from memory on paper.
> 4. Every topic now starts with a cartoon. The same pictures are saved as separate SVG files in `images/`.

## THE MASTER PICTURE: "The Restaurant Host"

![Cartoon: restaurant host as load balancer](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/00-master-restaurant-host.svg)*

Imagine a busy restaurant. **Everything in load balancing is this one scene.**

```
                    HUNGRY CUSTOMERS (requests)
                 o   o   o   o   o   o   o   o
                  \   \   |   |   |   /   /
                   v   v  v   v   v  v   v
              +--------------------------------+
              |   THE HOST AT THE DOOR (LB)    |   <- one stable entrance
              |  - reads the reservation (L7)  |
              |  - or just counts heads (L4)   |
              |  - peeks at each table (health)|
              +--------------------------------+
                  |          |          |
                  v          v          v
             +--------+ +--------+ +--------+
             | TABLE 1| | TABLE 2| | TABLE 3|     <- servers
             |  OK    | |  OK    | |  FAINTED|    <- failed waiter
             +--------+ +--------+ +--------+
                  \          |          /
                   +----------------------+
                   | SHARED ORDER TICKETS |        <- Redis / DB
                   | (any waiter can serve|           (stateless servers)
                   |  any customer)       |
                   +----------------------+

   BACKUP HOST stands ready behind the first one  (failover for the LB)
   MORE TABLES can be added on busy nights        (horizontal scaling)
```

**Mapping (memorize this table):**

| Restaurant | System |
|---|---|
| Customers | Client requests |
| Host at the door | Load balancer |
| Host counts heads only | L4 (IP + port) |
| Host reads the reservation notes | L7 (URL, headers, cookies) |
| Seats guests table 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 | Round robin |
| Seats guests at the emptiest table | Least connections |
| Host peeks into each table: "alive?" | Health check |
| A waiter faints, host stops sending guests there | Failover |
| Open more tables on busy nights | Horizontal scaling |
| Order tickets on a shared board | Stateless servers + Redis |
| One host, long queue at the door | LB bottleneck / SPOF |
| Several hosts + backup host | Redundant LBs |

### Order-of-topics mnemonic

The 8 topics in order: **W**hy, **L**4/L7, **R**ound robin, **L**east connections, **H**ealth checks, **F**ailover, **H**orizontal scaling, **B**ottlenecks.

> **"Wise Lions Run, Leave Hungry Foxes Hunting Birds."**
> **W L R L H F H B**

## TOPIC 1: Why load balancing is needed

![Cartoon: why load balancing](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/01-why-load-balancing.svg)*

### Picture: "One tired waiter vs a team"

```
WITHOUT LB                          WITH LB
                                                     +-> [Waiter 1]
 o o o o o o o o                    o o o o o o o o  |
   \ \ | | | / /                      \ \ | | | / /  +-> [Waiter 2]
    v v v v v v                        [  HOST  ] ----|
   [ ONE WAITER ]  <- collapses                       +-> [Waiter 3]
   [   X  DEAD  ]  <- everyone starves
```

### Interview answer (about 45 seconds)

> "A single server has a ceiling on CPU, memory, and connections, and it is also a single point of failure. You can scale vertically with a bigger machine, but that hits a hard limit, gets expensive, and still leaves one point of failure. So we scale horizontally with many servers, and the load balancer is what makes that work. It gives clients one stable address, spreads traffic across healthy servers, and hides how many servers exist. That gives us three things: capacity, availability, and the freedom to deploy or scale without clients noticing."

### Likely follow-up
**Q: Why not just buy a bigger server?**
A: Hardware ceiling, nonlinear cost, and it is still one failure away from a full outage.

### Recall hook
**"C-A-F"**: **C**apacity, **A**vailability, **F**lexibility. (Latency too: route to the closest or least busy.)

## TOPIC 2: L4 vs L7

![Cartoon: L4 vs L7](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/02-l4-vs-l7.svg)*

### Picture: "Counting heads vs reading the reservation"

```
   L4 HOST (fast, blind)                 L7 HOST (smart, slower)
   +---------------------+               +------------------------------+
   | Sees: IP + PORT     |               | Sees: URL, headers, cookies  |
   | "Party of 4 -> Tbl 2"|              | "Reservation says VEGAN       |
   | Doesn't read notes  |               |  -> Vegan table"             |
   +---------------------+               +------------------------------+
   NLB / TCP / UDP                        ALB / HTTP / HTTPS
```

**Layer cheat:** L4 = **T**ransport = **T**ickets only (IP/port). L7 = **A**pplication = **A**ll the details.

### Interview answer (about 60 seconds)

> "L4 load balancers work at the transport layer. They only look at IP address and port, and forward TCP or UDP connections without reading the content. That makes them very fast, cheap, and protocol-agnostic, so they suit raw throughput, non-HTTP protocols, and static IP needs. In AWS that's the NLB.
> L7 load balancers work at the application layer. They understand HTTP, so they can route by path, host, header, or cookie, terminate TLS, do auth and rate limiting. The cost is more CPU and a bit more latency. In AWS that's the ALB.
> I choose L7 when routing depends on request content, like `/api/orders` versus `/api/cart` in a microservices setup. I choose L4 for speed or non-HTTP traffic. Large systems often use both: L4 at the edge to absorb connections, L7 behind it for smart routing."

### Likely follow-up
**Q: Where does TLS terminate?**
A: Usually at the LB, to offload CPU and centralize certificates. Re-encrypt to backends if compliance needs end-to-end encryption.

### Recall hook
**L4 = Fast and Blind. L7 = Smart and Slower.** NLB = L4, ALB = L7 (the **A**pplication one).

## TOPIC 3: Round Robin

![Cartoon: round robin](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/03-round-robin.svg)*

### Picture: "The merry-go-round / dealing cards"

```
  Requests:   1    2    3    4    5    6
              |    |    |    |    |    |
              v    v    v    v    v    v
  Servers:   [A]  [B]  [C]  [A]  [B]  [C]   <- like dealing cards in turn

  PROBLEM: Card 2 is a HUGE order (slow request)
  [A]  [B: stuck on slow job...]  [C]
  Round robin still deals to B on its turn. It doesn't look.
```

### Interview answer (about 40 seconds)

> "Round robin sends requests to servers in rotation: one, two, three, one, two, three. It is simple, needs no state, and works well when servers are identical and requests cost roughly the same. Its weakness is that it ignores current load. If requests vary a lot in duration, or one server is slower, it keeps feeding that server its turn and it can pile up. A common variant is weighted round robin, where a server with double the capacity gets double the turns, but weights are static so it still doesn't adapt to live load."

### Likely follow-up
**Q: When does round robin break?**
A: Uneven request cost or uneven servers: a mix of long uploads and short API calls can stack long jobs on one server.

### Recall hook
**"Deal the cards in turn, never peek at the hand."**

---

## TOPIC 4: Least Connections

![Cartoon: least connections](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/04-least-connections.svg)*

### Picture: "The host seats guests at the emptiest table"

```
  Table A: [o o]                 <- 2 guests (long meals)
  Table B: [o o o o o o o o o o] <- 10 guests (short snacks)

  New guest arrives ---> Host looks at crowd size ---> sends to A
  (Round robin would have alternated blindly.)
```

### Interview answer (about 50 seconds)

> "Least connections sends each new request to the server with the fewest active connections. It adapts to real load, so it works well when request durations vary: file uploads, WebSockets, slow queries. For example, if server A has two long-running requests and server B has ten short ones, round robin keeps feeding both equally, while least connections favors the less loaded one.
> The trade-off is that the LB must track connection counts per server. In very large fleets I'd use 'power of two choices': pick two random servers and send to the less loaded. It gets nearly the same result with far less coordination."

### Likely follow-up
**Q: What if a server is slow but has few connections?**
A: Use least response time, passive health checks, outlier ejection, and timeouts.

### Recall hook
**"Count the crowd, pick the emptiest table."** Pair of two = "pick 2, take the lighter."

## TOPIC 5: Health Checks

![Cartoon: health checks](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/05-health-checks.svg)*

### Picture: "The host peeks into each table"

```
  ACTIVE (host walks over every 5 seconds):
     Host --"you alive?"--> [Table 1]  yes
     Host --"you alive?"--> [Table 2]  yes
     Host --"you alive?"--> [Table 3]  ... silence x3  -> mark OUT

  PASSIVE (host just watches the room):
     Sees plates crashing / guests complaining (5xx, timeouts) -> mark OUT

  RULE:  N fails -> OUT      M successes -> back IN
```

### Interview answer (about 60 seconds)

> "Health checks let the LB send traffic only to healthy servers. There are two kinds. Active checks: the LB calls an endpoint like `/health` every few seconds; after N consecutive failures the server is marked unhealthy and removed, and after M consecutive successes it returns. Passive checks: the LB watches real traffic and ejects servers returning 5xx or timing out.
> Tuning matters. Too aggressive causes flapping and extra load; too slow sends users to dead servers. I also keep health checks shallow. If `/health` checks the database and the DB goes down, every server fails and the LB has zero targets, turning a partial issue into a total outage. Dependency failures are better handled with timeouts, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation."

### Likely follow-up
**Q: What if all health checks fail?**
A: Some LBs fail open and route to all targets; another reason to keep checks shallow and to alert on fleet-wide failure.

### Recall hook
**"Knock on the door: N knocks unanswered = out, M answers = back in. Shallow knock only."**

## TOPIC 6: Failover

![Cartoon: failover](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/06-failover.svg)*

### Picture: "Fainted waiter + backup host"

```
  LEVEL 1: A SERVER dies               LEVEL 2: The LB dies
  [T1] [T2] [T3 X]                     [HOST] X      [BACKUP HOST] <- takes the
   host skips T3, retries guests         active          shared "door sign"
                                                        (virtual IP)
  LEVEL 3: The WHOLE RESTAURANT (region) burns
  Route 53 / DNS: "go to the other branch" (slower: DNS TTL)
```

### Interview answer (about 60 seconds)

> "Failover works at three levels. If a backend server fails, health checks detect it, the LB stops routing there, and requests go to the remaining servers. In-flight requests may fail and get retried elsewhere, which is only safe for idempotent operations.
> If the load balancer itself fails, we avoid a single point of failure with redundant LBs: active-passive with a shared virtual IP and heartbeat, or active-active across availability zones with DNS or anycast. Managed LBs like ALB and NLB do this for you.
> For a regional failure, DNS-level failover such as Route 53 health checks redirects to another region, but it's slower because of DNS TTL and caching."

### Likely follow-up
**Q: What happens to sessions on the dead server?**
A: Lost if stored in memory; preserved if sessions are in Redis or a JWT.

### Recall hook
**"Server, LB, Region: three layers of backup."** (S-L-R)

## TOPIC 7: Horizontal Scaling

![Cartoon: horizontal scaling](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/07-horizontal-scaling.svg)*

### Picture: "Add tables, and make order tickets shared"

```
  Quiet night:   [T1] [T2]
  Busy night:    [T1] [T2] [T3] [T4] [T5]   <- auto scaling adds tables

  Why it works: orders live on a SHARED BOARD, not in the waiter's head
                   [T1] [T2] [T3]
                      \   |   /
                    [ Redis / DB ]   <- any waiter can serve any guest
  Sticky sessions = "guest must always get the SAME waiter" (waiter faints -> order lost)
```

### Interview answer (about 60 seconds)

> "Horizontal scaling means adding more instances instead of a bigger one, and the load balancer is what lets us do it transparently. For it to work well, servers should be stateless: session data lives in Redis, a database, or a JWT, not in server memory. Then any server can handle any request, and we can add or remove instances freely.
> With auto scaling, metrics like CPU or request count trigger the Auto Scaling Group, new instances register with the LB, pass health checks, and start receiving traffic. On scale-in, connection draining lets in-flight requests finish before removal. If state can't be externalized, sticky sessions are a fallback, but they cause uneven load and lost sessions when a server dies."

### Likely follow-up
**Q: How do you do zero-downtime deploys?**
A: Connection draining, rolling or blue-green deployment, and health checks gating traffic to new instances.

### Recall hook
**"Stateless = Shared ticket board."** Scale out = add tables; scale in = let guests finish (drain).

---

## TOPIC 8: Load Balancer Bottlenecks

![Cartoon: load balancer bottlenecks](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/08-lb-bottlenecks.svg)*

### Picture: "One host, a long queue at the door"

```
   o o o o o o o o o o o o   <- queue outside!
        \  \  |  |  /  /
         [ ONE HOST ]        <- overwhelmed = SPOF + bottleneck
            |  |  |
          tables are idle

   FIX: layers of greeters
   Users -> [Geo DNS] -> [L4 LB x many] -> [L7 LB x many] -> Services
                                                             \-> service mesh inside
```

### Interview answer (about 60 seconds)

> "The load balancer can become the bottleneck or a single point of failure itself. I address that in layers. For availability: redundant LB nodes across AZs. For CPU limits from TLS handshakes and L7 parsing: offload or scale out LB nodes, and put a fast L4 tier in front of L7. For bandwidth and connection limits: multiple LB nodes with DNS or anycast spreading traffic. For the extra network hop on internal calls: client-side load balancing or a service mesh. And I prefer stateless algorithms, since shared state like sticky tables and connection tracking limits scaling.
> A typical big-system layering is geo-DNS, then L4, then L7, then services, with a service mesh internally."

### Likely follow-up
**Q: Is the LB a SPOF?**
A: Not if it is redundant across AZs with managed or active-active setup.

### Recall hook
**"Never one host: many hosts, layered, with a backup."**

## INTERVIEW FOCUS: "What happens when one server fails?"

![Cartoon: server failure 8-frame comic](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*(Image file: images/09-server-failure-comic.svg)*

### Picture: the 8-frame comic strip

```
 [1] NORMAL        [2] CRASH        [3] DETECT          [4] EJECT
  A  B  C            A  B(X) C       "B didn't answer     A      C
  all fed            B dies          3 knocks / errors"   (B removed)

 [5] RETRY          [6] PROTECT      [7] REPLACE          [8] REJOIN
 in-flight reqs     A and C take     auto scaling adds    B (or new one) passes
 to B retried       +50% load:       a new server,        M checks, then SLOW
 elsewhere          timeouts,        gets traffic         START ramp-up
 (idempotent!)      breakers,        slowly
                    jitter, shed
```

### Interview answer (about 90 seconds, the one to rehearse)

> "Let's say three servers A, B, C are behind the LB using least connections, and B crashes.
> **Detection:** either passively, because in-flight requests to B time out or error, or actively, because B fails N consecutive health checks; with 3 checks at 5-second intervals that's up to about 15 seconds.
> **Ejection:** the LB marks B unhealthy and sends new requests only to A and C.
> **User impact:** requests in flight to B may fail. The LB or client retries on another server, which is safe only for idempotent requests. If sessions were in B's memory they're lost, which is why I keep servers stateless with Redis sessions.
> **Survivor protection:** A and C now carry about 50% more load, so I protect them with timeouts, circuit breakers, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and load shedding, otherwise the failure can cascade.
> **Recovery:** auto scaling launches a replacement; once it passes health checks the LB adds it using slow start so it isn't hit with a full share instantly. If B itself recovers, it must pass M consecutive checks before rejoining.
> The goal is that one server failure is invisible to users, apart from a small window of retried requests."

### Follow-ups to prepare
| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| What if the LB dies? | Redundant LB nodes, multi-AZ, DNS or anycast |
| What if all health checks fail? | Fail-open behavior; keep checks shallow; alert |
| Slow but not dead server? | Least response time, outlier ejection, timeouts, circuit breakers |
| Why retry storms are dangerous | Everyone retries at once and overloads survivors; use backoff with jitter |

### Recall hook for the 8 frames
**"N-C-D-E-R-P-R-R"**: **N**ormal, **C**rash, **D**etect, **E**ject, **R**etry, **P**rotect, **R**eplace, **R**ejoin.
Sentence: **"Nobody Can Detect Every Rotten Pie, Right? Really!"**

## ONE-PAGE RECALL SHEET (redraw this from memory)

```
  Why?  -> One server = limit + SPOF.   C-A-F: Capacity, Availability, Flexibility
  L4/L7 -> Counting heads (fast) vs reading reservation (smart).  NLB / ALB
  RR    -> Deal cards in turn.  Breaks when requests are uneven.
  LC    -> Seat at emptiest table.  Needs tracking.  Power of 2 at huge scale.
  Health-> Knock N times = out, M answers = in.  Active + passive.  Keep shallow.
  Failover-> Server / LB / Region.  Retry only idempotent.  Sessions in Redis.
  Scale -> Stateless + shared ticket board.  Auto scale out, drain on scale in.
  Bottleneck-> Many hosts, layered: DNS -> L4 -> L7 -> services -> mesh.
```
